Trying to Conceive

Foods and Habits That Support Fertility

Updated: July 1, 2026

This article is shown in English while its translation is prepared.

No single food will make you conceive, but the overall pattern of what you eat and how you live influences hormonal balance, ovulation, and sperm health. Small, consistent habits are what matter.

Build meals around whole foods

Emphasize vegetables, fruit, whole grains, legumes, nuts, and healthy fats such as olive oil. Diets rich in these — sometimes described as Mediterranean-style — are associated with better reproductive health.

Choose good protein sources and include some plant proteins. Cutting back on heavily processed foods, sugary drinks, and trans fats is a simple, high-value change.

Key nutrients to prioritize

Folate, iron, iodine, vitamin D, omega-3 fats, and antioxidants all play roles in reproductive health. A varied diet plus a prenatal vitamin covers most bases.

Iron from plant sources is absorbed better alongside vitamin C, so pairing beans or greens with citrus or peppers is a helpful habit.

Aim for a healthy weight

Being significantly under or over a healthy weight can disrupt ovulation and lower fertility. You do not need to be "perfect" — even modest movement toward a healthy range can help regulate cycles.

Focus on sustainable habits rather than restrictive dieting, which can itself affect cycles.

Habits that help — and hurt

Regular moderate exercise, good sleep, and stress management support hormonal balance. Very intense over-exercising, on the other hand, can sometimes disrupt cycles.

Avoid smoking and recreational drugs, limit alcohol, and keep caffeine moderate. These affect both egg and sperm quality.

It takes two

Fertility is not only about the person carrying the pregnancy. A partner’s diet, weight, alcohol use, smoking, and heat exposure all affect sperm quality.

Making these changes together tends to be easier and more effective than going it alone.

Key takeaways

  • Favor a whole-food, Mediterranean-style pattern over processed foods.
  • Prioritize folate, iron, iodine, vitamin D, and omega-3s; a prenatal helps.
  • Aim for a healthy weight range to support regular ovulation.
  • Sleep, moderate exercise, and stress management support hormones.
  • Partners should adopt fertility-friendly habits too.

Frequently asked questions

Are there foods that boost fertility instantly?

No single food works like that. Consistent, balanced nutrition over weeks and months supports reproductive health far more than any one "superfood."

Should I cut out caffeine completely?

Most guidance suggests keeping caffeine moderate rather than eliminating it. Check current recommendations with your provider.

Does weight really affect fertility?

Yes — being well under or over a healthy weight can disrupt ovulation and reduce fertility, so moving toward a healthy range can help.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
